name: Lyndon B. Johnson
summary: A New Deal Democrat who, as Senate leader and president, expanded federal programs against poverty and for health care, schooling and civil rights, and signed consumer, gun and crime laws, while keeping a large military, the draft and an escalating war in Vietnam. In Congress he had voted against early civil rights bills and for Taft-Hartley, the 1950 Internal Security Act and the 1954 ban on the Communist Party, then drove the 1957 and 1960 civil rights acts and signed the 1964, 1965 and 1968 laws.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Built up the armed forces and stressed military strength.

arms-reduction.rationale: Listed controlling, reducing and 'ultimately eliminating' the engines of destruction as a principle of policy and worked on non-proliferation, while raising military spending for Vietnam.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: His record points both ways: he signed the 1964 income tax cut while the budget was in deficit, then the 1968 surcharge and spending limits to cut the deficit.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: In 1954 he voted for the Humphrey substitute to outlaw the Communist Party and for the Communist Control Act.

capital-controls.rationale: He signed the Interest Equalization Tax Act of 1964, which taxed Americans' purchases of foreign securities to curb the outflow of capital.

character-from-environment.rationale: Said ability 'is not just the product of birth' but is shaped by family, neighborhood, school and surroundings.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Built Medicare, Medicaid, education and anti-poverty programs as government responsibilities rather than leaving the poor to charity.

class-collaboration.rationale: Urged business, labor and consumers to cooperate on price and wage restraint.

collective-defense.rationale: He voted to ratify the North Atlantic Treaty and against the Watkins reservations that would have denied any US obligation under its Article V.

conscription.rationale: He voted for universal military training in 1951 (against striking it) and for the four-year draft extension in 1959 (against limiting it to two years), and as president signed the Military Selective Service Act of 1967.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Described American justice as a nation where each man 'could be ruled by the common consent of all' and framed the voting rights bill around the democratic right to vote.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: In the Great Society speech he wanted a society 'where men are more concerned with the quality of their goals than the quantity of their goods' and warned of a 'soulless wealth'.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Argued that freedom was not enough and that the next stage of civil rights was equality 'as a fact and as a result', with programs to overcome the legacy of slavery and oppression.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Proposed a 'substantial cut in excise taxes' in 1964 to leave more money with consumers; those were taxes on selected goods and services rather than general sales taxes.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He signed the Economic Opportunity Act and the Food Stamp Act in 1964 and Medicaid in 1965, expanding aid to the poor rather than cutting it.

decide-locally.rationale: Rejected 'purely local control over elections' and pressed national action on voting, civil rights and cities, though he spoke of 'creative federalism' with local leaders.

defeat-communism.rationale: Mixed: fought the war in Vietnam against Communist aggression and called Hanoi's aim a Communist takeover, yet pursued arms control, East-West trade and talks with the Soviets (Glassboro).

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: In 1956 he voted against two proposals to elect the President by direct popular vote and for a substitute keeping state electoral votes, divided in proportion to the popular vote or by district.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In 1950 he voted for adding emergency detention provisions to the internal security bill and for the Internal Security Act, which allowed detention of suspected saboteurs in an emergency, over Truman's veto.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He voted to ratify the North Atlantic Treaty (1949), the Korea defense treaty (1954) and the SEATO treaty (1955), and against reservations limiting the NATO commitment.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Mixed: at Howard he said opportunity alone was not enough, but on signing the Civil Rights Act he said it 'does not give special treatment to any citizen'. He did not address admissions or hiring preferences directly.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He signed the Civil Rights Acts of 1964 and 1968 and the Voting Rights Act, which forbid unequal treatment by race, color, religion or national origin.

equal-outcomes.rationale: At Howard he sought 'not just equality as a right and a theory but equality as a fact and equality as a result', while framing the goal as giving everyone the same chance; equal opportunity was 'essential, but not enough'.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He signed the 1965 immigration act abolishing the national-origins quotas that had favored northern Europeans, though in 1952 he voted to override Truman's veto of the McCarran-Walter Act that kept them.

farm-price-support.rationale: In 1951 he voted against the Williams amendment to suspend price supports on farm commodities, which was rejected 4-78.

force-without-un.rationale: He sought and signed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which authorised all necessary steps including armed force in Southeast Asia, and fought the war on that basis without a UN Security Council mandate.

free-trade.rationale: In Congress he mostly voted to extend the President's reciprocal trade-agreement authority (1940, 1943) and against amendments to end trade agreements, but also voted for import quotas on oil (1949) and furs.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: He signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars discrimination in public accommodations and employment, and the 1968 Act barring discrimination in housing.

future-generations.rationale: Called for a conservation effort to leave 'a green legacy for tomorrow' and warned that destroyed natural splendour can never be recaptured.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Said 'men and women of all races are born with the same range of abilities' and that ability is stunted or stretched by family, neighborhood and school.

legalize-drugs.rationale: He signed the Drug Abuse Control Amendments of 1965, which put depressant, stimulant and hallucinogenic drugs under federal control.

limit-guns.rationale: He signed the Gun Control Act of 1968, a law "to provide for better control of the interstate traffic in firearms".

limit-population.rationale: Offered help to nations trying to control population growth and said rapid population growth in developing countries must be slowed.

military-superiority.rationale: Said US military power was 'strong enough to meet any threat and destroy any adversary' and that its superiority would keep growing while he held office.

minority-language-support.rationale: He signed the Bilingual Education Act (Title VII of the 1967 education amendments), funding programs for children of limited English-speaking ability.

national-law-over-international.rationale: In 1954 he voted for the Ferguson amendment declaring that a treaty or international agreement provision that conflicts with the Constitution shall be of no effect, and for the George substitute, though he voted against Bricker's stronger version.

national-self-determination.rationale: He said Americans "cherish self-determination for all people" and justified the defence of South Vietnam as its right to choose its own course.

positive-liberty.rationale: Said 'freedom is not enough': citizens must have the ability to walk through the gates of opportunity, so he sought jobs, schooling, housing and health care.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: He voted for the 1941 price control bill and in 1943 against barring price control on food commodities below parity.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: He voted for wartime price control in 1941 and in 1950-1952 against amendments removing the Korean War price and wage stabilization titles.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Declared a war on poverty and made ending poverty a central goal of his administration; the Economic Opportunity programs and Great Society targeted the poor.

property-franchise.rationale: He voted in 1960 for the Holland amendment to ban poll taxes and property qualifications in federal elections and signed the 1965 Voting Rights Act against poll taxes; in the House (1942-1947) he had voted against anti-poll-tax bills, a position his later record replaced.

public-access-to-information.rationale: He signed the Freedom of Information Act of 1966, which makes agency records available to any person and lets the courts enforce it.

public-service-media.rationale: He signed the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, which created a federally funded nonprofit corporation, not a government agency, to protect public broadcasting "from extraneous interference and control".

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: He signed the 1965 act ending the national-origins quota system, after voting in 1952 to enact the McCarran-Walter Act over Truman's veto, which retained it.

racial-franchise.rationale: He signed the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which bans denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race or color.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: He signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banning segregation in public accommodations and the 1968 Act banning housing discrimination; in 1950 he had voted for an amendment letting enlistees choose units of their own race, a position his later sustained record replaced.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Named the heritage of slavery, oppression and 'present prejudice' as a main cause of Black poverty, alongside inherited poverty, and said the gap was widening 'despite the court orders and the laws'.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: He voted for the 1960 bill raising the minimum wage from $1 to $1.25 and signed the 1966 amendments raising it to $1.60 and extending coverage; in 1949 he had backed an amendment letting rates stay between 55 and 75 cents.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He signed new federal rules for business: motor vehicle safety standards (1966), packaging and labeling rules (1966) and truth-in-lending disclosure (1968).

rehabilitation.rationale: He signed the Prisoner Rehabilitation Act of 1965, which let federal prisoners live in residential treatment centers and go out to paid work or training.

rent-control.rationale: He voted repeatedly to keep federal rent ceilings (1949-1952), including against a 1951 amendment ending maximum rents where localities declared a housing shortage.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: He voted for Taft-Hartley's strike and boycott restrictions (1947), for presidential strike injunctions (1949) and the Landrum-Griffin Act (1959), and as president signed a 1967 law settling a rail dispute that barred resort to strike.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: He voted for the Marshall Plan (1948), Point Four technical aid (1950) and Mutual Security Acts and appropriations from 1951 to 1960, and against a 1952 amendment restricting Point Four spending.

space-expansion.rationale: In 1958 he told the Senate that "the exploration of outer space will dominate the affairs of mankind" and moved a committee on national space policy; calling it the central goal of civilization goes beyond what he said.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Said the Great Society should meet the 'needs of the spirit' and build 'a richer life of mind and spirit'.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: He voted to ratify NATO and SEATO, joining the United States to the Western bloc's military alliances.

surveillance-ok.rationale: He signed the Omnibus Crime Control Act of 1968, whose Title III authorised court-ordered wiretapping and kept the President's national security surveillance power.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Mixed: the War on Poverty targeted the poor, while Medicare and education aid were broad programs for the elderly or all schools.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He voted to extend tariff-cutting trade agreements and against ending them, but supported import quotas protecting domestic oil and furs in 1949, so his record is mixed toward liberal trade.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: He signed the Revenue Act of 1964, which cut the top individual rate to 70 percent, and in 1951 voted against raising the capital-gains rate, although in the 1940s he voted against Republican tax cuts.

term-limits.rationale: In 1947 he voted against the constitutional amendment limiting a President to two terms.

traditional-family.rationale: Called the family 'the cornerstone of our society' and urged policy to keep parents together.

unions-good.rationale: Called labor an 'indispensable force in the American system' (1964) and asked Congress to repeal Taft-Hartley section 14(b) (1966).

universal-healthcare.rationale: He voted for the 1960 Anderson amendment to give Social Security retirees medical benefits and signed Medicare and Medicaid in 1965, covering the aged and the poor; he never enacted coverage for everyone, so the fit is partial.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: In 1947 he voted against the 22nd Amendment, which ended unlimited presidential re-election.

work-for-welfare.rationale: He signed the 1967 Social Security Amendments, which created a work incentive program and had states refer able welfare recipients to work or training, with sanctions for refusing without good cause.

notes: Pass 2 (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-07, rules 4): every source tagged action or words; answers with a record (his House and Senate roll calls 1937-1960 from Voteview, and laws he signed, cited from the Statutes at Large on GovInfo) were re-sourced to the record alone and their earlier word-based versions kept in reviewHistory. Over time: he voted against anti-lynching and anti-poll-tax bills in the House and for a 1950 segregated-units amendment, then supported the 1957 and 1960 acts, the 1960 anti-poll-tax amendment and signed the 1964-68 laws; the later sustained record is used. Themes searched: economy (taxes, wages, labor, price and rent controls, trade, capital), government (term limits, electoral college, treaties, internal security), world (alliances, aid, Vietnam, Dominican Republic), liberty (drugs, prisons, wiretaps, information), society and culture (immigration, language, race), ecology and technology (oil depletion, space, pollution). Searched: Voteview roll calls (all 3,038 of his votes), the Stanford parsed Congressional Record (his floor speeches 1937-1960), the Miller Center speeches, and his signed statutes. A 1958 floor passage defending the oil depletion allowance was left out because it is an inserted statement by another speaker (it refers to '18 years on the Senate Finance Committee'). presidency.ucsb.edu's robots.txt now disallows ClaudeBot, so new presidential texts were taken from the Miller Center corpus and GovInfo instead. Vietnam: he escalated the war after the Tonkin Gulf Resolution (1964) and on March 31, 1968 limited the bombing and said he would not seek reelection.
